new_en: 40) There, "and the Levi pours water," etc. Thus it is taught at the end of Zohar, Parashat Nasso, 146a: A kohen who wishes to spread his hands must add sanctity to his sanctity, and must sanctify his hands through a sanctified hand. What is the sanctified hand? It is the Levi, from whose hand the kohen must receive the sanctification of the water, as it is written, "You shall sanctify the Levites," so they are sanctified. It is also written concerning the Levites, "And also your brethren, the tribe of Levi," etc. From here we learn that every kohen who spreads his hands must be sanctified through one who is sanctified, in order to add sanctity to his sanctity, and therefore he should not receive the sanctification of the water from another person who does not have this sanctity. In Tzeniuta DeSifra it is taught that a Levi through whom a kohen is sanctified must first sanctify himself. Why specifically a Levi, and why should the kohen not be sanctified through another kohen? It is taught that another kohen should not do so, because a kohen who is not whole should not cause a whole kohen to be impaired through one who is deficient. A Levi who is whole, however, and is fit to ascend to the duchan and to serve in the Mishkan, is whole and is called sanctified, as it is written, "You shall sanctify the Levites." Beit Yosef cites this, and this is the basis of the Mechaber's words here in Shulchan Aruch. The words of the Zohar imply that if no Levi is present, the kohen should not have an Israelite or another kohen wash his hands, but should wash them himself. Bach, however, writes in the name of Maharil that where no Levites are present, if there is a firstborn who opened the womb, he should pour water for the kohanim to wash before ascending to the duchan. This is cited by Knesset HaGedolah, Hagahot Beit Yosef, letter 3; Olat Tamid, letter 13; Taz, seif katan 3; Ateret Zekenim, letter 1; Magen Avraham, seif katan 7; and Eliyah Rabbah, letter 10. Magen Avraham writes that Maharil's language implies specifically a maternal firstborn, but a paternal firstborn alone has no recognized sanctity nowadays. This is cited by Shaliach Tzibbur, page 143a; Shulchan Aruch HaRav, letter 10; Chayei Adam, rule 32, letter 8; Chesed LaAlafim, letter 3; Beit Menuchah, letter 11; and Ben Ish Chai, Parashat Tetzaveh, letter 7. I have not seen anyone practice this. It appears that they rely upon the plain implication of the Zohar, that specifically a Levi should pour, and if no Levi is present the kohen washes his own hands.

There, only for leniency, that grape pits are permitted. The language of the Gemara there, 26b, is that it derives that an intoxicated kohen is forbidden to recite the Priestly Blessing from the juxtaposition of the section of the Priestly Blessing to the section of a nazir: just as a nazir is forbidden wine, so too a kohen who blesses. The Gemara asks: if so, just as a nazir is forbidden grape pits, should a kohen who blesses also be forbidden them? It answers from the verse, "to serve Him and to bless in His Name": just as one who serves is permitted grape pits, so too a kohen who blesses. It then asks: just as a blemished kohen may not serve, should a blemished kohen also not bless? It answers that the kohen who blesses was compared to a nazir. Why choose the comparison for leniency rather than for stringency? It answers that these comparisons are only an asmachta, and in a rabbinic matter we rule leniently.

The custom is not to perform Nefilat Apayim in a house of mourning, etc., even when a Sefer Torah is present. Another reason is to avoid arousing and strengthening the attribute of judgment. Accordingly, Selichot are recited in a house of mourning, but not Vidui or supplications. On the day of a brit milah, Tachanun is omitted specifically at Shacharit. Some say it is omitted even at Minchah. [Maharshal] This means when praying in the presence of the infant upon whom the brit milah was performed, and this is the practice in the community of Brisk in Lithuania. In the presence of a groom, however, Tachanun is omitted throughout the day. [Hagahot Maimoniyot, chapter 5 of the Laws of Prayer]

The mourner. Meaning, no supplication is recited there at all. Lamnatzeach Shir Mizmor is also not recited, but "Vezot Beriti Otam" is recited. Maharil writes that Hallel is not recited there even on Chanukah. Tanya, however, writes that only on Rosh Chodesh is Hallel omitted, because its recitation then is only a custom, whereas on Chanukah Hallel is recited. Magen Avraham writes that on Chanukah it is proper for each person to recite Hallel at home, and Ran writes likewise. See Taz, who writes in seif katan 9 that VeHu Rachum, which is said on Monday and Thursday, should be recited at home by the other worshippers after they leave the mourner's house. Rachum VeChanun, however, should not be recited at all, even at home; see there for the reason.

On the day of a brit milah. The authorities disagree whether the omission of Tachanun in the presence of the infant applies only at Shacharit or also at Minchah. The custom in Brisk of Lithuania and in Krakow is to omit it also at Minchah, and it appears proper to be lenient because Nefilat Apayim is optional. Taz and Knesset HaGedolah write accordingly; see Magen Avraham. Eliyah Rabbah writes that if they pray Minchah in the presence of the infant after Birkat HaMazon was already recited following the festive meal, it is possible that Tachanun should be recited, because one may rely upon Rama in this matter.

To the chuppah. Knesset HaGedolah writes that the statement that he is considered a groom only on the day he enters the chuppah is intended only to exclude the period before he enters the chuppah. Once he has entered the chuppah, Nefilat Apayim is omitted for all 7 days if he comes to the synagogue, and certainly when he prays at home. Whether a bachelor married a virgin, a bachelor married a widow, or a widower married a virgin, Nefilat Apayim is omitted for 7 days from the chuppah wherever they pray. If a widower married a widow, it is omitted only during the first 3 days of marriage; afterward it is recited. Pri Chadash and Taz rule likewise. Taz concludes that throughout all 7 days of celebration the groom should not come to the synagogue, so that the congregation will not thereby refrain from reciting Tachanun. On the wedding day itself, even if the chuppah will not take place until evening, Terumat HaDeshen, siman 80, holds that Nefilat Apayim is omitted at Shacharit. Pri Chadash disagrees and writes that as long as he has not entered the chuppah, Nefilat Apayim is recited. See Knesset HaGedolah, Magen Avraham, and Halachot Ketanot, part 1, siman 21.

The custom is not to perform Nefilat Apayim in a house of mourning, in a groom's house, in the synagogue on the day of a brit milah, or when a groom is present there. {Rama: This applies specifically when the brit milah or the groom is in that same synagogue. But if the brit milah is not in that synagogue, even though it takes place in another synagogue in the city, Tachanun is recited. [Piskei Mahari'a, siman 81] On the day of a brit milah, when Tachanun is omitted, this applies only at Shacharit, when the brit milah is performed. At Minchah, even if they pray in the presence of the infant after the brit milah, Tachanun is recited. This differs from a groom, in whose presence Tachanun is omitted throughout the day. [Hagahot Maimoniyot, chapter 5 of the Laws of Prayer] One is called a groom for this purpose only on the day he enters the chuppah.}
